questions.q: A load of $10 \text{ kg}$ is suspended by a metal wire that is $3 \text{ m}$ long and possesses a cross-sectional area of $4 \text{ mm}^2$. Determine the stress. The Young modulus of the metal is $2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given mass of the load, $m = 10 \text{ kg}$

Cross-sectional area, $A = 4 \text{ mm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

The restoring force developed in the wire is equal to the weight of the suspended load.

$F = mg = 10 \times 9.8 = 98 \text{ N}$

Stress is defined as the restoring force per unit area.

$\text{Stress} = \dfrac{F}{A}$

$\text{Stress} = \dfrac{98}{4 \times 10^{-6}} = 24.5 \times 10^6 \text{ N/m}^2$

$\text{Stress} = 2.45 \times 10^7 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vertical metal cylinder of radius $2 \text{ cm}$ and length $2 \text{ m}$ is fixed at its lower end, and a load of $100 \text{ kg}$ is placed on it. Determine the stress. The Young modulus of the metal is $2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
The stress on the cylinder is given by the ratio of the applied force to the cross-sectional area.

Force applied by the load, $F = mg = 100 \times 10 = 1000 \text{ N}$

Cross-sectional area, $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (2 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 4\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

$\text{Stress} = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{1000}{4\pi \times 10^{-4}}$

$\text{Stress} = \dfrac{10^7}{4\pi} \approx 7.96 \times 10^5 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.q: A vertical metal cylinder of radius $2 \text{ cm}$ and length $2 \text{ m}$ is fixed at its lower end, and a load of $100 \text{ kg}$ is placed on it. Determine the strain. The Young modulus of the metal is $2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given:
Radius of the cylinder, $r = 2 \text{ cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$
Mass of the load, $m = 100 \text{ kg}$
Young's modulus, $Y = 2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g \approx 10 \text{ m/s}^2$

The force applied on the cylinder is:
$F = mg = 100 \times 10 = 1000 \text{ N}$

The cross-sectional area of the cylinder is:
$A = \pi r^2 = \pi (2 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 4\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

The strain is given by the formula:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{F}{AY}$

Substituting the values:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{1000}{4\pi \times 10^{-4} \times 2 \times 10^{11}}$

$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{1000}{8\pi \times 10^7} = \dfrac{1}{8\pi} \times 10^{-4}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:
$\text{Strain} \approx \dfrac{1}{25.12} \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.0398 \times 10^{-4} \approx 4 \times 10^{-6}$

questions.solution:
The force applied on the wire is the weight of the load:
$F = mg = 10 \times 9.8 = 98 \text{ N}$

The cross-sectional area is:
$A = 4 \text{ mm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$

The formula for Young's modulus is:
$Y = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \dfrac{F / A}{\text{Strain}}$

Rearranging for strain:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{F}{A \cdot Y}$

Substituting the given values:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{98}{4 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.0 \times 10^{11}}$

$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{98}{8 \times 10^5}$

$\text{Strain} = 12.25 \times 10^{-5} = 1.225 \times 10^{-4}$

$L = 3 \text{ m}$
$A = 4 \text{ mm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$
$Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$
$g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

The force applied on the wire is $F = mg = 10 \times 9.8 = 98 \text{ N}$.

The elongation $\Delta L$ is given by the formula:
$\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$

Substituting the values:
$\Delta L = \dfrac{98 \times 3}{4 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.0 \times 10^{11}}$

$\Delta L = \dfrac{294}{8 \times 10^5}$

questions.q: A vertical metal cylinder of radius $2 \text{ cm}$ and length $2 \text{ m}$ is fixed at its lower end, and a load of $100 \text{ kg}$ is placed on it. Determine the compression of the cylinder. The Young modulus of the metal is $2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
The compression of the cylinder is given by the formula for Young's modulus:

$Y = \dfrac{F L}{A \Delta L} \Rightarrow \Delta L = \dfrac{F L}{A Y}$

The force applied is the weight of the load. Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$F = mg = 100 \times 10 = 1000 \text{ N}$

The cross-sectional area of the cylinder is:

$A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (2 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 4\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

Substituting the given values into the formula:

$\Delta L = \dfrac{1000 \times 2}{4\pi \times 10^{-4} \times 2 \times 10^{11}}$

$\Delta L = \dfrac{2000}{8\pi \times 10^7}$

$\Delta L = \dfrac{250}{\pi} \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$\Delta L \approx 79.6 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \approx 8 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Steel has an elastic limit of $8 \times 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$ and a Young modulus of $2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$. Determine the maximum elongation that can be produced in a half-metre steel wire without exceeding its elastic limit.
questions.solution:
Given:

Elastic limit (maximum stress), $\sigma = 8 \times 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$

Young's modulus, $Y = 2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$

Length of the wire, $L = 0.5 \text{ m}$

From the definition of Young's modulus:

$Y = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\Delta L / L}$

Rearranging for maximum elongation $\Delta L$:

$\Delta L = \dfrac{\sigma \times L}{Y}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta L = \dfrac{8 \times 10^8 \times 0.5}{2 \times 10^{11}}$

$\Delta L = \dfrac{4 \times 10^8}{2 \times 10^{11}}$

$\Delta L = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

$\Delta L = 2 \text{ mm}$

questions.q: A steel wire and a copper wire, both possessing equal length and equal cross-sectional area, are joined end to end and the combination is subjected to a tension. Determine the ratio of the strain developed in the copper wire to the strain developed in the steel wire. Let $Y$ of steel $= 2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$ and $Y$ of copper $= 1.3 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let $F$ be the tension applied to the combination of the wires. Since the wires are joined end to end, the tension $F$ is the same in both wires.

The cross-sectional area $A$ is also the same for both wires. Therefore, the stress $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A}$ is equal for both the steel and copper wires.

Young's modulus is given by $Y = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$, which implies $\text{Strain} = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{Y}$.

Let $\epsilon_c$ and $\epsilon_s$ be the strains developed in the copper and steel wires, respectively.

$\epsilon_c = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y_c}$

$\epsilon_s = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y_s}$

Taking the ratio of the strain in copper to the strain in steel:

$\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_s} = \dfrac{Y_s}{Y_c}$

Substituting the given values, $Y_s = 2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$ and $Y_c = 1.3 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$:

$\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_s} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{11}}{1.3 \times 10^{11}} = \dfrac{20}{13}$

questions.solution:
Stress is defined as the internal restoring force per unit area.

When the wires are joined end to end and subjected to a tension, they are in a series combination. Therefore, the same force $F$ acts on both the steel and copper wires.

It is given that both wires have the same cross-sectional area $A$.

The stress in the steel wire is $\sigma_{s} = \dfrac{F}{A}$.

The stress in the copper wire is $\sigma_{c} = \dfrac{F}{A}$.

The ratio of the stress developed in the steel wire to that in the copper wire is $\dfrac{\sigma_{s}}{\sigma_{c}} = \dfrac{F/A}{F/A} = 1$.

questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, the upper wire is constructed from steel and the lower wire from copper. Both wires possess an equal cross section. Determine the ratio of the longitudinal strain developed in the copper wire to that in the steel wire.
questions.solution:
Both the steel and copper wires are connected in series and support the same load, so they experience the same tension $T$.

Given that both wires have an equal cross-sectional area $A$, the longitudinal stress $\sigma$ in both wires is the same:

$\sigma = \dfrac{T}{A}$

From Hooke's law, the longitudinal strain $\epsilon$ is given by:

$\epsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y}$

where $Y$ is the Young's modulus of the material. The ratio of the longitudinal strain in the copper wire to that in the steel wire is:

$\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_s} = \dfrac{\sigma / Y_c}{\sigma / Y_s} = \dfrac{Y_s}{Y_c}$

Using the standard values of Young's modulus for steel and copper:
$Y_s = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$
$Y_c = 1.3 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$

Substituting these values into the ratio:

$\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_s} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{11}}{1.3 \times 10^{11}} = \dfrac{20}{13} \approx 1.538$

Rounding to two decimal places, we get $1.54$.

Answer: $1.54$

questions.q: The two wires depicted in the figure are constructed from the same material, which possesses a breaking stress of $8 imes 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$. The cross-sectional area of the upper wire is $0.006 \text{ cm}^2$ and that of the lower wire is $0.003 \text{ cm}^2$. Given that the mass $m_1 = 10 \text{ kg}$, $m_2 = 20 \text{ kg}$ and the hanger is light, determine the maximum load that can be placed on the hanger without breaking a wire. Also, state which wire will break first if the load is increased. (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let $M$ be the mass of the load placed on the hanger.

The tension in the lower wire is given by $T_1 = (m_1 + M)g = (10 + M) \times 10$.

The tension in the upper wire is given by $T_2 = (m_1 + m_2 + M)g = (10 + 20 + M) \times 10 = (30 + M) \times 10$.

The cross-sectional area of the lower wire is $A_1 = 0.003 \text{ cm}^2 = 3 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.

The cross-sectional area of the upper wire is $A_2 = 0.006 \text{ cm}^2 = 6 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.

The breaking stress for both wires is $\sigma_{\text{max}} = 8 \times 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$.

For the lower wire not to break, the stress must be less than or equal to the breaking stress:

$\dfrac{T_1}{A_1} \le \sigma_{\text{max}}$

$\dfrac{(10 + M) \times 10}{3 \times 10^{-7}} \le 8 \times 10^8$

$100 + 10M \le 240$

$10M \le 140 \Rightarrow M \le 14 \text{ kg}$

For the upper wire not to break, the stress must be less than or equal to the breaking stress:

$\dfrac{T_2}{A_2} \le \sigma_{\text{max}}$

$\dfrac{(30 + M) \times 10}{6 \times 10^{-7}} \le 8 \times 10^8$

$300 + 10M \le 480$

$10M \le 180 \Rightarrow M \le 18 \text{ kg}$

The maximum load that can be placed without breaking either wire is the minimum of the two values, which is $14 \text{ kg}$.

Since the maximum load limit for the lower wire is reached first, the lower wire will break first if the load is increased beyond $14 \text{ kg}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An upper wire hangs from a ceiling and supports a mass $m_2 = 36 \text{ kg}$. A lower wire hangs from $m_2$ and supports a mass $m_1 = 10 \text{ kg}$. A light hanger is attached below $m_1$. Both wires are made of the same material having a breaking stress of $8 imes 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$. The area of cross section for the upper wire is $0.006 \text{ cm}^2$ while that for the lower wire is $0.003 \text{ cm}^2$. Calculate the maximum load that can be added to the hanger without breaking a wire, and identify which wire will break first if the load is further increased. (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of the load added to the hanger.

The tension in the lower wire is given by the total weight it supports:
$T_1 = (m_1 + m)g = (10 + m) \times 10$

The tension in the upper wire is given by the total weight it supports:
$T_2 = (m_2 + m_1 + m)g = (36 + 10 + m) \times 10 = (46 + m) \times 10$

The maximum tension the lower wire can withstand before breaking is:
$T_{1, \text\max} = \text{Breaking stress} \times A_1$
$T_{1, \text\max} = (8 \times 10^8) \times (0.003 \times 10^{-4}) = 240 \text{ N}$

The maximum tension the upper wire can withstand before breaking is:
$T_{2, \text\max} = \text{Breaking stress} \times A_2$
$T_{2, \text\max} = (8 \times 10^8) \times (0.006 \times 10^{-4}) = 480 \text{ N}$

For the lower wire not to break:
$(10 + m) \times 10 \le 240$
$10 + m \le 24 \Rightarrow m \le 14 \text{ kg}$

For the upper wire not to break:
$(46 + m) \times 10 \le 480$
$46 + m \le 48 \Rightarrow m \le 2 \text{ kg}$

The maximum load that can be added without breaking either wire is the smaller of the two values, which is $2 \text{ kg}$.

If the load is further increased beyond $2 \text{ kg}$, the tension in the upper wire will exceed its maximum capacity first. Therefore, the upper wire will break first.

questions.solution:

The Young modulus is given by $Y = \dfrac{F L}{A \Delta L}$.

Substituting the values:

$Y = \dfrac{100 \times 2}{2 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{-2}}$

$Y = \dfrac{200}{2 \times 10^{-6}}$

$Y = 1 \times 10^8 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.q: Consider the setup illustrated in the figure. The applied force $F$ is equal to $m_2 g/2$. Assuming the string is light and there is no friction present anywhere, determine the strain developed in the string if its cross-sectional area is $A$ and its Young modulus is $Y$.
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the acceleration of the system and $T$ be the tension in the string.

Assuming the block of mass $m_2$ moves downwards and $m_1$ moves to the right, the equations of motion are:
For mass $m_2$:
$m_2 g - T = m_2 a$

For mass $m_1$:
$T - F = m_1 a$

Adding the two equations, we get:
$m_2 g - F = (m_1 + m_2) a$

Given that $F = \dfrac{m_2 g}{2}$, substituting this into the equation:
$m_2 g - \dfrac{m_2 g}{2} = (m_1 + m_2) a$

$\dfrac{m_2 g}{2} = (m_1 + m_2) a$

$a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{2(m_1 + m_2)}$

Now, substituting the value of $a$ in the equation for $m_2$ to find the tension $T$:
$T = m_2 g - m_2 a$

$T = m_2 g - m_2 \left( \dfrac{m_2 g}{2(m_1 + m_2)} \right)$

$T = m_2 g \left( 1 - \dfrac{m_2}{2(m_1 + m_2)} \right)$

$T = m_2 g \left( \dfrac{2m_1 + 2m_2 - m_2}{2(m_1 + m_2)} \right)$

$T = \dfrac{m_2 g (2m_1 + m_2)}{2(m_1 + m_2)}$

The strain developed in the string is given by the ratio of stress to Young's modulus:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{T}{A Y}$

Substituting the value of $T$:
$\text{Strain} = \dfrac{m_2 g (2m_1 + m_2)}{2 A Y (m_1 + m_2)}$

questions.q: A steel wire with an initial length of $1 \text{ m}$ and a cross-sectional area of $4.00 \text{ mm}^2$ is secured at both ends such that it remains horizontal and tension-free. When a $2.16 \text{ kg}$ load is hung from the wire's midpoint, what will be its vertical depression? Use $Y$ for steel $= 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$ and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let the initial length of the wire be $2l = 1 \text{ m}$, so $l = 0.5 \text{ m}$.

Let $x$ be the vertical depression at the midpoint.

The new length of each half of the wire is $l' = \sqrt{l^2 + x^2}$.

The change in length of each half is $\Delta l = \sqrt{l^2 + x^2} - l \approx l \left(1 + \dfrac{x^2}{2l^2}\right) - l = \dfrac{x^2}{2l}$.

The longitudinal strain in the wire is $\epsilon = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \dfrac{x^2}{2l^2}$.

The tension $T$ in the wire is given by $T = Y A \epsilon = \dfrac{Y A x^2}{2l^2}$.

For equilibrium at the midpoint, the vertical components of the tension balance the weight of the load:

$2 T \sin \theta = m g$

where $\sin \theta = \dfrac{x}{l'} \approx \dfrac{x}{l}$.

Substituting $T$ and $\sin \theta$:

$2 \left( \dfrac{Y A x^2}{2l^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{x}{l} \right) = m g$

$\dfrac{Y A x^3}{l^3} = m g$

$x^3 = \dfrac{m g l^3}{Y A}$

Substituting the given values $m = 2.16 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, $l = 0.5 \text{ m}$, $Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$, and $A = 4.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$:

$x^3 = \dfrac{2.16 \times 10 \times (0.5)^3}{2.0 \times 10^{11} \times 4.00 \times 10^{-6}}$

$x^3 = \dfrac{21.6 \times 0.125}{8.0 \times 10^5}$

$x^3 = \dfrac{2.7}{8.0 \times 10^5} = \dfrac{27}{8} \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3$

Taking the cube root of both sides:

$x = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 1.5 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal wire of unstretched length $4 \text{ m}$ and diameter $1 \text{ mm}$ suspends a sphere of mass $20 \text{ kg}$. At equilibrium, a clear gap of $2 \text{ mm}$ is present between the sphere and the floor. The sphere is gently pulled aside until the wire forms an angle $\theta$ with the vertical, and is then released. Determine the maximum value of $\theta$ such that the sphere avoids rubbing the floor. The Young modulus of the wire's metal is $2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$. Make appropriate approximations.
questions.solution:
Let the original unstretched length of the wire be $L$.

At equilibrium, the tension in the wire is $T_0 = mg$.

The elongation of the wire at equilibrium is:

$\Delta L_0 = \dfrac{mgL}{AY}$

When the sphere passes through the lowest point (mean position) after being released from an angle $\theta$, its velocity $v$ is given by conservation of energy:

$v^2 = 2gL(1 - \cos\theta)$

The tension $T$ at the lowest point is:

$T = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{L} = mg + 2mg(1 - \cos\theta)$

For the sphere to just avoid rubbing the floor, the maximum elongation of the wire at the lowest point must be $\Delta L = \Delta L_0 + h$, where $h$ is the equilibrium gap.

The tension can also be expressed using Hooke's law for this maximum elongation:

$T = \dfrac{YA\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{YA}{L}\left(\dfrac{mgL}{AY} + h\right) = mg + \dfrac{YAh}{L}$

Equating the two expressions for tension $T$:

$mg + 2mg(1 - \cos\theta) = mg + \dfrac{YAh}{L}$

$2mg(1 - \cos\theta) = \dfrac{YAh}{L}$

$1 - \cos\theta = \dfrac{YAh}{2mgL}$

Given values are:
$Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$
$d = 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m} \Rightarrow A = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$
$h = 2 \text{ mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
$m = 20 \text{ kg}$
$L = 4 \text{ m}$

Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$1 - \cos\theta = \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{11}) \times \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 10^{-6}\right) \times (2 \times 10^{-3})}{2 \times 20 \times 10 \times 4}$

$1 - \cos\theta = \dfrac{100\pi}{1600} = \dfrac{\pi}{16} \approx \dfrac{3.1416}{16} \approx 0.196$

$\cos\theta \approx 1 - 0.196 = 0.804$

$\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.804) \approx 36.4^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Determine the decrease in the cross-sectional area of a copper wire having an initial cross-sectional area of $0.01 \text{ cm}^2$ that is subjected to a tension of $20 \text{ N}$. The Young modulus of copper is $1.1 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$ and its Poisson ratio is $0.32$.
[Hint: $\dfrac{\Delta A}{A} = 2 \dfrac{\Delta r}{r}$]
questions.solution:
The longitudinal strain in the wire is given by $\dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{F}{AY}$

The lateral strain is given by $\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} = \sigma \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{\sigma F}{AY}$

The fractional change in the cross-sectional area is $\dfrac{\Delta A}{A} = 2 \dfrac{\Delta r}{r} = \dfrac{2\sigma F}{AY}$

The decrease in the cross-sectional area is $\Delta A = A \left( \dfrac{2\sigma F}{AY} \right) = \dfrac{2\sigma F}{Y}$

Substituting the given values $F = 20 \text{ N}$, $\sigma = 0.32$, and $Y = 1.1 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$:

$\Delta A = \dfrac{2 \times 0.32 \times 20}{1.1 \times 10^{11}} \text{ m}^2$

$\Delta A = \dfrac{12.8}{1.1} \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}^2 = 11.636 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}^2$

Converting to $\text{cm}^2$:

$\Delta A = 11.636 \times 10^{-11} \times 10^4 \text{ cm}^2 \approx 1.164 \times 10^{-6} \text{ cm}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the increase in pressure needed to reduce the volume of a water sample by $0.01\%$. The bulk modulus of water is $2.1 \times 10^9 \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
The bulk modulus $B$ is defined as:

$B = \dfrac{\Delta P}{\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}}$

Given the percentage reduction in volume is $0.01\%$, the fractional change in volume is:

$\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{0.01}{100} = 10^{-4}$

The bulk modulus of water is $B = 2.1 \times 10^9 \text{ N/m}^2$.

The required increase in pressure $\Delta P$ is:

$\Delta P = B \times \dfrac{\Delta V}{V}$

$\Delta P = (2.1 \times 10^9) \times 10^{-4}$

$\Delta P = 2.1 \times 10^5 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the estimated change in the density of water in the ocean at a depth of $400 \text{ m}$ below the surface. The density of water at the surface is $1030 \text{ kg/m}^3$ and the bulk modulus of water is $2 \times 10^9 \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
The change in pressure at a depth $h$ is given by:

$\Delta P = \rho g h$

The bulk modulus $B$ relates the change in pressure to the fractional change in density:

$B = \dfrac{\Delta P}{\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho}}$

Rearranging for the change in density $\Delta \rho$:

$\Delta \rho = \dfrac{\rho \Delta P}{B} = \dfrac{\rho^2 g h}{B}$

Substituting the given values (using $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$):

$\Delta \rho = \dfrac{(1030)^2 \times 9.8 \times 400}{2 \times 10^9}$

$\Delta \rho = \dfrac{1060900 \times 3920}{2 \times 10^9}$

$\Delta \rho = \dfrac{4.158 \times 10^9}{2 \times 10^9}$

$\Delta \rho \approx 2.08 \text{ kg/m}^3$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated change in density is $2 \text{ kg/m}^3$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The lower surface of a steel plate having a face area of $4 \text{ cm}^2$ and a thickness of $0.5 \text{ cm}$ is fixed rigidly. A tangential force of $10 \text{ N}$ is applied to the upper surface. Determine the lateral displacement of the upper surface relative to the lower surface. The rigidity modulus of steel is $8.4 \times 10^{10} \text{ N/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given, tangential force $F = 10 \text{ N}$

Face area $A = 4 \text{ cm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

Thickness $L = 0.5 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$

Rigidity modulus $\eta = 8.4 \times 10^{10} \text{ N/m}^2$

The formula for rigidity modulus is given by:

$\eta = \dfrac{\text{Shear Stress}}{\text{Shear Strain}} = \dfrac{F / A}{\Delta x / L}$

Rearranging for lateral displacement $\Delta x$:

$\Delta x = \dfrac{F L}{A \eta}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta x = \dfrac{10 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-2}}{4 \times 10^{-4} \times 8.4 \times 10^{10}}$

$\Delta x = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-2}}{33.6 \times 10^6}$

$\Delta x = \dfrac{5}{33.6} \times 10^{-8}$

$\Delta x \approx 1.488 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$\Delta x \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight piece of thread, $5.0 \text{ cm}$ in length, is placed on the surface of water. Determine the force with which the surface on one side of the thread pulls it. The surface tension of water is given as $0.076 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
Length of the thread, $l = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$

Surface tension of water, $S = 0.076 \text{ N/m}$

The force exerted by the surface of water on one side of the thread is given by:

$F = S \times l$

$F = 0.076 \times 0.05 = 0.0038 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the excess pressure inside a drop of mercury having a radius of $2 \text{ mm}$. The surface tension of mercury is given as $0.465 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
The excess pressure inside a liquid drop is given by the formula $\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{R}$.

Given:
$T = 0.465 \text{ N/m}$
$R = 2 \text{ mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Substituting the values in the formula:
$\Delta P = \dfrac{2 \times 0.465}{2 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\Delta P = 0.465 \times 10^3$

$\Delta P = 465 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the excess pressure inside a soap bubble having a radius of $4 \text{ mm}$. The surface tension of the soap solution is given as $0.03 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
The excess pressure inside a soap bubble is given by the formula:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{4T}{R}$

where $T$ is the surface tension and $R$ is the radius of the bubble.

Given $T = 0.03 \text{ N/m}$ and $R = 4 \text{ mm} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{4 \times 0.03}{4 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\Delta P = \dfrac{0.03}{10^{-3}} = 30 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the excess pressure inside an air bubble of radius $4 \text{ mm}$ formed within a tank of water. The surface tension of water is given as $0.076 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
The excess pressure inside an air bubble formed within a liquid is given by the formula:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{R}$

where $T$ is the surface tension of the liquid and $R$ is the radius of the bubble.

Given:
$T = 0.076 \text{ N/m}$
$R = 4 \text{ mm} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{2 \times 0.076}{4 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\Delta P = \dfrac{0.152}{4 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\Delta P = 38 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a small surface area of $1 \text{ mm}^2$ at the top of a mercury drop of radius $4.0 \text{ mm}$. Determine the force exerted on this area by the air above it. Atmospheric pressure is $1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$ and surface tension of mercury is $0.465 \text{ N/m}$. Neglect the effect of gravity. Assume all numbers to be exact.
questions.solution:
The pressure exerted by the air above the mercury drop is the atmospheric pressure, $P_0 = 1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$.

The given surface area on the drop is $A = 1 \text{ mm}^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$.

The force exerted by the air on this area is calculated as:

$F = P_0 \times A$

$F = (1.0 \times 10^5) \times (1.0 \times 10^{-6}) = 0.1 \text{ N}$

The surface tension and radius of the drop are not required to find the force exerted by the outside air, as they are used to determine the pressure inside the drop.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a small surface area of $1 \text{ mm}^2$ at the top of a mercury drop of radius $4.0 \text{ mm}$. Determine the force exerted on this area by the mercury below it. Atmospheric pressure is $1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$ and surface tension of mercury is $0.465 \text{ N/m}$. Neglect the effect of gravity. Assume all numbers to be exact.
questions.solution:
The pressure inside the mercury drop is given by $P = P_0 + \dfrac{2T}{R}$, where $P_0$ is the atmospheric pressure, $T$ is the surface tension, and $R$ is the radius of the drop.

Given:
$P_0 = 1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$
$T = 0.465 \text{ N/m}$
$R = 4.0 \text{ mm} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

The excess pressure inside the drop is:
$\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{R} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.465}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 232.5 \text{ Pa}$

The total pressure of the mercury just inside the surface is:
$P = P_0 + \Delta P = 100000 + 232.5 = 100232.5 \text{ Pa}$

The force exerted by the mercury below the small surface area $A = 1 \text{ mm}^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$ is due to this internal pressure:
$F = P \times A = 100232.5 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6} = 0.1002325 \text{ N}$

Rounding to five decimal places, we get $F \approx 0.10023 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a small surface area of $1 \text{ mm}^2$ at the top of a mercury drop of radius $4.0 \text{ mm}$. Determine the force exerted on this area by the mercury surface in contact with it. Atmospheric pressure is $1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$ and surface tension of mercury is $0.465 \text{ N/m}$. Neglect the effect of gravity. Assume all numbers to be exact.
questions.solution:
For a small area $\Delta A$ on the surface of a liquid drop in equilibrium, the outward force due to the pressure inside the drop is balanced by the inward force due to atmospheric pressure and the inward resultant force exerted by the surrounding surface due to surface tension.

Let $P_{in}$ be the pressure inside the drop and $P_0$ be the atmospheric pressure. The excess pressure is given by:

$P_{ex} = P_{in} - P_0 = \dfrac{2T}{R}$

The force exerted by the surrounding mercury surface on the small area $\Delta A$ is the resultant of the surface tension forces, which is directed radially inward. For equilibrium of the area $\Delta A$:

$P_{in} \Delta A = P_0 \Delta A + F_s$

$F_s = (P_{in} - P_0) \Delta A = P_{ex} \Delta A = \dfrac{2T}{R} \Delta A$

Given:
$T = 0.465 \text{ N/m}$
$R = 4.0 \text{ mm} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
$\Delta A = 1 \text{ mm}^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$

Substituting the values:

$F_s = \dfrac{2 \times 0.465}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$

$F_s = \dfrac{0.93}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} \times 10^{-6} = 232.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$

$F_s = 0.0002325 \text{ N} \approx 0.00023 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The capillaries displayed in the figure possess inner radii of $0.5 \text{ mm}$, $1.0 \text{ mm}$ and $1.5 \text{ mm}$ respectively. The liquid contained within the beaker is water. Determine the heights of the water level in the capillaries. The surface tension of water is $7.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$.
options: $3 \text{ cm}$ in $A$, $1.5 \text{ cm}$ in $B$, $1 \text{ cm}$ in $C$
$1.5 \text{ cm}$ in $A$, $0.75 \text{ cm}$ in $B$, $0.5 \text{ cm}$ in $C$
$1 \text{ cm}$ in $A$, $1.5 \text{ cm}$ in $B$, $3 \text{ cm}$ in $C$
$6 \text{ cm}$ in $A$, $3 \text{ cm}$ in $B$, $2 \text{ cm}$ in $C$
questions.solution:
The height of liquid in a capillary tube is given by Jurin's law:

$h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{\rho g r}$

For water and glass, the angle of contact $\theta \approx 0^{\circ}$, so $\cos \theta = 1$.
Density of water, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
Surface tension, $T = 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$.

For capillary A, $r_A = 0.5 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$:
$h_A = \dfrac{2 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 1}{1000 \times 10 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{15 \times 10^{-2}}{5} = 3 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 3 \text{ cm}$

For capillary B, $r_B = 1.0 \text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$:
$h_B = \dfrac{2 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 1}{1000 \times 10 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{15 \times 10^{-2}}{10} = 1.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 1.5 \text{ cm}$

For capillary C, $r_C = 1.5 \text{ mm} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$:
$h_C = \dfrac{2 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 1}{1000 \times 10 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{15 \times 10^{-2}}{15} = 1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 1 \text{ cm}$
questions.question: The capillaries displayed in the figure possess inner radii of $0.5 \text{ mm}$, $1.0 \text{ mm}$ and $1.5 \text{ mm}$ respectively. The liquid contained within the beaker is water. Determine the heights of the water level in the capillaries. The surface tension of water is $7.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$.
questions.explanation:
The height of liquid in a capillary tube is given by Jurin's law:

$h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{\rho g r}$

For water and glass, the angle of contact $\theta \approx 0^{\circ}$, so $\cos \theta = 1$.
Density of water, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
Surface tension, $T = 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$.

For capillary A, $r_A = 0.5 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$:
$h_A = \dfrac{2 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 1}{1000 \times 10 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{15 \times 10^{-2}}{5} = 3 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 3 \text{ cm}$

For capillary B, $r_B = 1.0 \text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$:
$h_B = \dfrac{2 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 1}{1000 \times 10 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{15 \times 10^{-2}}{10} = 1.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 1.5 \text{ cm}$

For capillary C, $r_C = 1.5 \text{ mm} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capillary tube has its lower end immersed in mercury, and the mercury level inside the tube is observed to be $2 \text{ cm}$ below the outside level. If this identical tube is immersed in water, to what height will the water rise in the capillary?
questions.solution:
The height of a liquid in a capillary tube is given by Jurin's law:

$h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$

For mercury, the capillary fall is:

$h_{Hg} = \dfrac{2T_{Hg} \cos \theta_{Hg}}{r \rho_{Hg} g} = -2 \text{ cm}$

For water, the capillary rise is:

$h_w = \dfrac{2T_w \cos \theta_w}{r \rho_w g}$

Taking the ratio of the two heights to eliminate the radius $r$ and acceleration due to gravity $g$:

$\dfrac{h_w}{h_{Hg}} = \left( \dfrac{T_w}{T_{Hg}} \right) \times \left( $\dfrac{\rho_{Hg}}{\rho_w} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{\cos \theta_w}{\cos \theta_{Hg}} \right)

Using the standard physical constants for water and mercury:
Surface tension of water, $T_w \approx 0.075 \text{ N/m}$
Surface tension of mercury, $T_{Hg} \approx 0.465 \text{ N/m}$
Density of water, $\rho_w = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$
Density of mercury, $\rho_{Hg} = 13600 \text{ kg/m}^3$
Angle of contact for water, $\theta_w = 0^{\circ} \Rightarrow \cos 0^{\circ} = 1$
Angle of contact for mercury, $\theta_{Hg} \approx 140^{\circ} \Rightarrow \cos 140^{\circ} \approx -0.766$

Substituting these values into the ratio equation:

\dfrac{h_w}{-2} = \left( \dfrac{0.075}{0.465} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{13600}{1000} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{-0.766} \right)$

$h_w = -2 \times \dfrac{0.075}{0.465} \times 13.6 \times \dfrac{1}{-0.766}$

$h_w = \dfrac{2.04}{0.35619} \approx 5.727 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to two decimal places, the water will rise to a height of $5.73 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: $5.73 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A barometer is constructed using a tube of radius $1.0 \text{ mm}$. Assuming the surface of the mercury in the tube has a spherical shape, determine the height raised in the barometer tube if the atmospheric pressure is equal to $76 \text{ cm}$ of mercury. The contact angle of mercury with glass is $135^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ and the surface tension of mercury is $0.465 \text{ N/m}$. The density of mercury is $13600 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
questions.solution:
The atmospheric pressure corresponds to a mercury column of height $h_0 = 76 \text{ cm}$.

Due to surface tension, the mercury level in the tube experiences a capillary depression. The capillary rise (or depression) is given by:

$h_c = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$

Substituting the given values:
$T = 0.465 \text{ N/m}$
$\theta = 135^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \Rightarrow \cos 135^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -0.707$
$r = 1.0 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
$\rho = 13600 \text{ kg/m}^3$
$g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

$h_c = \dfrac{2 \times 0.465 \times (-0.707)}{10^{-3} \times 13600 \times 9.8}$

$h_c = -\dfrac{0.6575}{133.28} \approx -0.00493 \text{ m} = -0.493 \text{ cm} \approx -0.5 \text{ cm}$

The actual height of the mercury column in the barometer is:

$h = h_0 + h_c = 76 \text{ cm} - 0.5 \text{ cm} = 75.5 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capillary tube with a radius of $0.50 \text{ mm}$ is vertically dipped into a pot of water. Find the difference between the pressure of the water inside the tube $5.0 \text{ cm}$ below the surface and the atmospheric pressure. The surface tension of water is $0.075 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
The pressure just below the meniscus in the capillary tube is given by $P_0 - \dfrac{2T}{r}$, where $P_0$ is the atmospheric pressure, $T$ is the surface tension, and $r$ is the radius of the tube.

The pressure $P$ at a depth $h$ below the meniscus inside the tube is:

$P = P_0 - \dfrac{2T}{r} + \rho g h$

The difference between this pressure and the atmospheric pressure is:

$\Delta P = P - P_0 = \rho g h - \dfrac{2T}{r}$

Given values are:

$\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$

$g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

$h = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$

$T = 0.075 \text{ N/m}$

$r = 0.50 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Calculating the hydrostatic pressure term:

$\rho g h = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 0.05 = 490 \text{ N/m}^2$

Calculating the capillary pressure term:

$\dfrac{2T}{r} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.075}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 300 \text{ N/m}^2$

Substituting these values into the pressure difference equation:

$\Delta P = 490 - 300 = 190 \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the surface energy of water contained in a cylindrical vessel with a radius of $6.0 \text{ cm}$. The surface tension of water is $0.075 \text{ J/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
The surface energy of a liquid is given by the product of its surface tension and the area of its free surface.

The free surface of water in a cylindrical vessel is circular. The area of this surface is:

$A = \pi r^2$

Given the radius $r = 6.0 \text{ cm} = 6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, the area is:

$A = \pi \times (6 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 36\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

The surface tension of water is $T = 0.075 \text{ J/m}^2$.

The surface energy $E$ is:

$E = T \times A$

$E = 0.075 \times 36\pi \times 10^{-4}$

$E = 2.7\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$E \approx 2.7 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J} = 8.478 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$

Rounding off, we get:

$E \approx 8.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A drop of mercury of radius $2 \text{ mm}$ is split into $8$ identical droplets. Determine the increase in surface energy. The surface tension of mercury is $0.465 \text{ J/m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the large drop be $R = 2 \text{ mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ and the radius of each small droplet be $r$.

From the conservation of volume:

$\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 8 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$

$R^3 = 8r^3 \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{R}{2}$

Initial surface area of the drop is $A_1 = 4\pi R^2$.

Final surface area of the $8$ droplets is $A_2 = 8 \times 4\pi r^2 = 32\pi \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 = 8\pi R^2$.

Increase in surface area is $\Delta A = A_2 - A_1 = 8\pi R^2 - 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi R^2$.

Increase in surface energy is given by $\Delta U = T \Delta A$, where $T$ is the surface tension.

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta U = 0.465 \times 4\pi (2 \times 10^{-3})^2$

$\Delta U = 0.465 \times 16\pi \times 10^{-6}$

$\Delta U = 7.44\pi \times 10^{-6}$

$\Delta U \approx 23.37 \times 10^{-6} \text{ J} = 2.34 \times 10^{-5} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capillary tube of radius $1 \text{ mm}$ is held vertical with the lower end in water. Determine the height of water raised in the capillary. If the length of the capillary tube is half of this calculated height, find the angle $\theta$ made by the water surface in the capillary with the wall.
questions.solution:
The height of water raised in a capillary tube is given by Jurin's law:

$h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{\rho g r}$

For water, assuming standard values $T = 0.075 \text{ N/m}$, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, and angle of contact $\theta = 0^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$:

$h = \dfrac{2 \times 0.075 \times \cos 0^{}^{{}^{\circ}}}{1000 \times 10 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.015 \text{ m} = 1.5 \text{ cm}$

When the capillary tube is of insufficient length $h'$, the water rises to the top and the meniscus adjusts its angle of contact to $\theta'$ such that the radius of curvature $R$ changes, keeping $h R$ constant. Since $R = \dfrac{r}{\cos \theta}$, we have:

$\dfrac{h}{\cos \theta} = \dfrac{h'}{\cos \theta'}$

Given that the new length is half of the calculated height, $h' = \dfrac{h}{2}$:

$\dfrac{h}{1} = \dfrac{h/2}{\cos \theta'}$

$\cos \theta' = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\theta' = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The lower end of a capillary tube of radius $1 \text{ mm}$ is dipped vertically into mercury. Determine the depression of the mercury column in the capillary. Furthermore, if the length dipped inside is half of this depression, find the angle made by the mercury surface at the end of the capillary with the vertical. The surface tension of mercury is $0.465 \text{ N/m}$ and the contact angle of mercury with glass is $135^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.
questions.solution:
The formula for the capillary depression $h$ of a liquid is given by:

$h = \dfrac{2T \cos(180^\circ - \theta)}{\rho g r}$

Substituting the given values ($T = 0.465 \text{ N/m}$, $\theta = 135^\circ$, $\rho = 13600 \text{ kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, $r = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$):

$h = \dfrac{2 \times 0.465 \times \cos 45^\circ}{13600 \times 9.8 \times 10^{-3}}$

$h = \dfrac{0.93 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{133.28} \approx 0.00493 \text{ m} = 4.93 \text{ mm}$

When the tube is dipped to a depth $l$ which is less than the natural depression $h$, the mercury meniscus stays at the lower end of the tube and adjusts its contact angle to a new value $\theta'$ to balance the pressure. The new depth is related to $\theta'$ by:

$l = \dfrac{2T \cos(180^\circ - \theta')}{\rho g r}$

Given that the length dipped is half of the natural depression ($l = \dfrac{h}{2}$), we get:

$\dfrac{2T \cos(180^\circ - \theta')}{\rho g r} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( $\dfrac{2T \cos(180^\circ - \theta)}{\rho g r} \right)

$\cos(180^\circ - \theta') = $\dfrac{1}{2} \cos($180^\circ - 135^\circ) = $\dfrac{1}{2} \cos$45^\circ$

$\cos(180^\circ - \theta') = $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx$0.3535$

This gives $180^\circ - \theta' \approx 69.3^\circ$.

The angle made by the mercury surface with the vertical (which is the new angle of contact $\theta'$) is:

$\theta' = 180^\circ - 69.3^\circ = 110.7^\circ \approx 111^\circ$

Thus, the depression is $4.93 \text{ mm}$ and the angle is $111^\circ$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two large glass plates are placed vertically and parallel to one another inside a tank of water, with a separation of $1 \text{ mm}$ between the plates. Determine the rise of water in the space between the plates. The surface tension of water is $0.075 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the plates be $L$ and the separation between them be $d$.

The upward force due to surface tension acts along the length of the two plates. Assuming the angle of contact for water and glass to be $\theta = 0^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$, the upward force is given by:

$F = 2TL \cos\theta = 2TL$

The weight of the water column raised to a height $h$ is:

$W = \text{volume} \times \rho \times g = (Ldh)\rho g$

At equilibrium, the upward force balances the weight of the water column:

$2TL = Ldh\rho g$

$h = \dfrac{2T}{\rho g d}$

Given $T = 0.075 \text{ N/m}$, $d = 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, and taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$h = \dfrac{2 \times 0.075}{1000 \times 10 \times 10^{-3}}$

$h = \dfrac{0.15}{10} = 0.015 \text{ m} = 1.5 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider an ice cube of edge $1.0 \text{ cm}$ placed in a gravity-free hall. Determine the surface area of the water after the ice melts. Ignore the difference in densities between ice and water.
questions.solution:
Volume of the ice cube is $V = a^3 = (1.0)^3 = 1.0 \text{ cm}^3$.

Since the difference in densities is ignored, the volume of water formed is also $V = 1.0 \text{ cm}^3$.

In a gravity-free space, the liquid takes a spherical shape to minimize its surface area due to surface tension.

Let the radius of the spherical water drop be $R$. Equating the volumes:

$\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 1$

$R = \left(\dfrac{3}{4\pi}\right)^{1/3}$

The surface area of the spherical drop is given by $A = 4\pi R^2$.

$A = 4\pi \left(\dfrac{3}{4\pi}\right)^{2/3}$

$A = (4\pi)^{1 - 2/3} (3^2)^{1/3}$

$A = (4\pi)^{1/3} (9)^{1/3} = (36\pi)^{1/3} \text{ cm}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire forming a loop is submerged into a soap solution and removed, establishing a film of soap solution. A loop of thread $6.28 \text{ cm}$ long is gently placed on the film, and the film is subsequently pricked with a needle inside the loop. The thread loop assumes a circular shape. Determine the tension in the thread. The surface tension of the soap solution is $0.030 \text{ N/m}$.
questions.solution:
The length of the thread loop is given by $L = 2\pi R = 6.28 \text{ cm} = 6.28 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

The radius of the circular loop is $R = \dfrac{6.28 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 3.14} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

When the film inside the loop is pricked, the outer soap film pulls the thread radially outward. Since a soap film has two free surfaces, the outward force per unit length is $2S$, where $S$ is the surface tension.

Considering a small element of the thread subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the center, the outward force on this element is $dF = (2S)(R d\theta)$.

This outward force is balanced by the inward radial component of the tension $T$ in the thread. The inward force is $2T \sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) \approx T d\theta$.

Equating the forces:

$T d\theta = 2S R d\theta$

$T = 2SR$

Substituting the given values $S = 0.030 \text{ N/m}$ and $R = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$:

$T = 2 \times 0.030 \times 10^{-2} = 6.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Falling vertically in glycerine, a metal sphere has a mass of $50 \text{ mg}$ and a radius of $1 \text{ mm}$. The coefficient of viscosity for glycerine at room temperature is $8.0 \text{ poise}$ and its density is $1260 \text{ kg/m}^3$. Determine the viscous force exerted on the sphere by the glycerine when the sphere reaches a speed of $1 \text{ cm/s}$.
questions.solution:
The viscous force acting on a spherical body falling through a viscous medium is given by Stokes' law:

$F = 6 \pi \eta r v$

Given parameters are:
Coefficient of viscosity, $\eta = 8.0 \text{ poise} = 0.8 \text{ Pa s}$
Radius of the sphere, $r = 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
Speed of the sphere, $v = 1 \text{ cm/s} = 10^{-2} \text{ m/s}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$F = 6 \times 3.14 \times 0.8 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-2}$

$F = 15.07 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}$

$F \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

The mass of the sphere and the density of glycerine are extraneous information for finding the viscous force at a specific speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Falling vertically in glycerine, a metal sphere has a mass of $50 \text{ mg}$ and a radius of $1 \text{ mm}$. The coefficient of viscosity for glycerine at room temperature is $8.0 \text{ poise}$ and its density is $1260 \text{ kg/m}^3$. Determine the hydrostatic force exerted on the sphere by the glycerine.
questions.solution:
The hydrostatic force exerted by the fluid on the sphere is the buoyant force acting on it.

The formula for buoyant force is given by:
$F_B = V \rho g$

Where:
$V$ is the volume of the sphere $= \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$
$\rho$ is the density of the fluid (glycerine) $= 1260 \text{ kg/m}^3$
$g$ is the acceleration due to gravity $= 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$
$r$ is the radius of the sphere $= 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Substituting the values into the formula:
$F_B = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi (10^{-3})^3 \times 1260 \times 9.8$

$F_B = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10^{-9} \times 1260 \times 9.8$

$F_B = 4 \times 22 \times 60 \times 9.8 \times 10^{-9}$

$F_B = 5280 \times 9.8 \times 10^{-9}$

$F_B = 51744 \times 10^{-9} \text{ N}$

$F_B = 5.1744 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}$

Rounding off to two significant figures, we get:
$F_B \approx 5.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Falling vertically in glycerine, a metal sphere has a mass of $50 \text{ mg}$ and a radius of $1 \text{ mm}$. The coefficient of viscosity for glycerine at room temperature is $8.0 \text{ poise}$ and its density is $1260 \text{ kg/m}^3$. Determine the terminal velocity at which the sphere will travel downward without acceleration.
questions.solution:
Given:
Mass of the sphere, $m = 50 \text{ mg} = 50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$
Radius of the sphere, $r = 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
Coefficient of viscosity, $\eta = 8.0 \text{ poise} = 0.8 \text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$
Density of glycerine, $\rho = 1260 \text{ kg/m}^3$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

Volume of the sphere, $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$

Buoyant force, $F_B = V\rho g = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$

Weight of the sphere, $W = mg$

At terminal velocity $v_t$, the net downward force is balanced by the viscous drag force (Stokes' law):

$6\pi\eta r v_t = W - F_B$

$v_t = \dfrac{mg - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g}{6\pi\eta r}$

Calculating the mass of displaced glycerine:
$m' = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (10^{-3})^3 \times 1260 = 5.28 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$

Net downward force:
$W - F_B = (50 \times 10^{-6} - 5.28 \times 10^{-6}) \times 9.8 = 44.72 \times 10^{-6} \times 9.8 = 4.38 \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

Viscous drag coefficient:
$6\pi\eta r = 6 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.8 \times 10^{-3} = 1.51 \times 10^{-2} \text{ kg/s}$

Terminal velocity:
$v_t = \dfrac{4.38 \times 10^{-4}}{1.51 \times 10^{-2}} = 2.9 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m/s} = 2.9 \text{ cm/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Using the following data, estimate the speed of vertically falling raindrops: radius of the drops $= 0.02 \text{ cm}$, viscosity of air $= 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ poise}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, and density of water $= 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
questions.solution:
The terminal velocity $v_t$ of a spherical drop falling through a viscous medium is given by Stokes' law:

$v_t = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{\eta}$

Given:
Radius of the raindrop, $r = 0.02 \text{ cm} = 2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$
Density of water, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$
Density of air, $\sigma \approx 0$ (negligible compared to water)
Viscosity of air, $\eta = 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ poise} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5} \text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ (since $1 \text{ poise} = 0.1 \text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$)
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$v_t = \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{(2 \times 10^{-4})^2 \times 1000 \times 10}{1.8 \times 10^{-5}}$

$v_t = \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^4}{1.8 \times 10^{-5}}$

$v_t = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-4}}{16.2 \times 10^{-5}}$

$v_t = \dfrac{80}{16.2} \approx 4.94 \text{ m/s}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the speed of the vertically falling raindrops is approximately $5 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water flows at a speed of $6 \text{ cm/s}$ through a tube having a radius of $1 \text{ cm}$. The coefficient of viscosity of water at room temperature is $0.01 \text{ poise}$. Compute the Reynolds number and determine if the flow is steady.
questions.solution:
The Reynolds number is given by the formula:

$R_e = \dfrac{\rho v D}{\eta}$

Given:
Speed of water, $v = 6 \text{ cm/s}$
Radius of the tube, $r = 1 \text{ cm} \Rightarrow \text{Diameter}, D = 2 \text{ cm}$
Coefficient of viscosity, $\eta = 0.01 \text{ poise}$
Density of water, $\rho = 1 \text{ g/cm}^3$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$R_e = \dfrac{1 \times 6 \times 2}{0.01} = 1200$

For flow through a pipe, if the Reynolds number is less than $2000$, the flow is considered steady (laminar). Since $R_e = 1200 < 2000$, the flow is steady.
